## Financial Accounts of the United States - Z.1

### Recent Developments [RSS](/feeds/z1.html) [Data Download](/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=z1)

The recent developments discussed below refer to data
through June 30, 2026.

**The net worth of households and nonprofit
organizations increased by $12.8 trillion** in the
second quarter of 2026, primarily driven by strong capital
gains on corporate equity assets.

**The debt of households and nonprofit
organizations increased 5.0%** at a seasonally
adjusted annual rate in the second quarter as the pace of
mortgage borrowing picked up and nonmortgage consumer credit
continued to grow at a moderate pace.

**Domestic nonfinancial business debt expanded
4.6%** at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in the
second quarter, reflecting solid growth in corporate bonds
and loan liabilities.

#### Household net worth

The net worth of households and nonprofit organizations –
the difference between the value of total assets and
liabilities (figure 1) – increased by $12.8 trillion to
$195.9 trillion in the second quarter.[1](#fn1) The ratio
of net worth to disposable personal income (DPI), a measure
of households’ potential to finance consumption out of their
wealth, reached a record high of 8.28 in the second quarter
(figure 2), surpassing the previous peak recorded in
2022:Q1.

##### Figure 1: Household balance sheet

![Figure depicts how the balance sheet of households changes over time](img/Household_balance_sheet_g.svg)

Note: Liabilities are shown as negative values. Corporate equities and debt securities include both directly held securities and securities held indirectly in mutual funds, defined contribution pension plans, and variable life insurance and annuity products. Deposits include money market fund shares. Real estate is the value of owner-occupied real estate. Other assets include consumer durable goods, fixed assets of nonprofit organizations, equity in noncorporate business, hedge fund shares, and all other assets apart from those shown.  
Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, September 11, 2026.

##### Figure 2: Ratio of household net worth to DPI

![Figure depicts how the ratio of household net worth to disposable income changes over time](img/Ratio_of_household_net_worth_to_DPI_g.svg)

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, September 11, 2026.

history_script.title: The Nineteen Thirty-Two Bonus Army March and Eviction
history_script.description: An examination of the nineteen thirty-two Bonus Army march on Washington, the military eviction ordered by General Douglas MacArthur, and the political fallout that reshaped American veterans' relief.
history_script.why_us: This focuses on a precise historical event utilizing verified National Archives images and source documents without relying on general institutional overviews.
history_script.timely_basis: The topic is presented as an evergreen historical analysis adhering strictly to archival documentation from nineteen thirty-two.

scenes.narration: In nineteen thirty-two, thousands of impoverished World War I veterans camped in Washington asking for early bonus payments.
scenes.visual_query: historic shanty town tents dirt road

scenes.narration: Demonstrators built temporary shelters on the Anacostia flats and occupied vacant government buildings near the Capitol.
As economic pressures dragged on, the House passed a relief bill while the Senate soundly rejected the payout.

diagram.title: Legislative Bonus Bill Path
diagram.note: Protesters remained in camps after the Senate rejected early payment.

scenes.narration: When police attempted evictions from vacant buildings, scuffles escalated into fatal police gunfire near the capital.
General Douglas MacArthur led cavalry, infantry, and tanks to clear the protesters against presidential orders.
Troops deployed tear gas and set fire to makeshift shanties, destroying the encampments across the flats.
Public outrage over the military crackdown damaged Hoover's campaign and eventually led Congress to fund the bonuses.

diagram.title: Political and Legislative Aftermath
diagram.note: Public reaction shifted politics and secured later relief.

issues: Scene 6: The photograph shows a peaceful camp scene with veterans sitting under an American flag, which contradicts the narration describing active destruction, tear gas, and burning shanties.

checks.claim: In nineteen thirty-two, thousands of impoverished World War I veterans camped in Washington asking for early bonus payments.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 2 confirm that in 1932, tens of thousands of impoverished WWI veterans traveled to Washington, D.C., to demand early payment of military bonuses scheduled for 1945.

checks.claim: Demonstrators built temporary shelters on the Anacostia flats and occupied vacant government buildings near the Capitol.
checks.explanation: Source 1 notes that protesters set up multiple camps near the Capitol and on the Anacostia flats, while Source 3 confirms they camped by the Anacostia River and occupied vacant buildings.

checks.claim: As economic pressures dragged on, the House passed a relief bill while the Senate soundly rejected the payout, and protesters remained in camps after the Senate rejected early payment.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 2 state that on June 15 the House passed the bonus bill and on June 17 the Senate defeated it, and Source 1 confirms marchers vowed to remain.

checks.claim: When police attempted evictions from vacant buildings, scuffles escalated into fatal police gunfire near the capital.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 6 note that on July 28 police attempted to evict veterans from abandoned buildings, scuffles broke out, and police gunfire killed two veterans.

checks.claim: General Douglas MacArthur led cavalry, infantry, and tanks to clear the protesters against presidential orders.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 6 detail that General MacArthur commanded troops (cavalry, infantry, and tanks) to clear the encampments, ignoring President Hoover's direct order not to pursue protesters across the bridge.

checks.claim: Troops deployed tear gas and set fire to makeshift shanties, destroying the encampments across the flats.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 3 confirm that troops launched tear gas attacks and burned the shanties and settlements to ensure protesters could not return.

checks.claim: Public outrage over the military crackdown damaged Hoover's campaign and eventually led Congress to fund the bonuses.
checks.explanation: Source 1 and Source 3 state that the attack damaged Hoover's reelection campaign, and Congress later passed legislation in 1936 to issue the bonuses.
